pages.description: Learn how to navigate A Tour of Go, run and edit example programs, format code, and use keyboard shortcuts while experimenting interactively.
Find available translations of A Tour of Go and learn how to continue through the tour using its navigation controls.
Install and run the standalone Go tour on your own computer for offline access to its lessons and code samples.
Understand how the Go Playground compiles and runs programs in a sandbox, including its deterministic time and resource restrictions.
Complete the first tour module and choose another module from the lesson list or proceed directly to the next lesson.
Learn how Go programs are organised into packages, why execution begins in package main, and how package names relate to import paths.
Group multiple Go imports in a parenthesized factored import statement, the preferred alternative to separate import declarations.
Understand how capitalization exports Go names and why code outside a package can access only that package's exported identifiers.
Define Go functions with zero or more arguments and place each parameter's type after its variable name.
Shorten consecutive Go function parameters that share a type by writing the type only after the final parameter name.
Return multiple results from a Go function, illustrated by a function that exchanges and returns two string values.
Use named return values to document result meanings and understand when a naked return helps or harms readability.
Declare typed variables with var at either package or function scope, following Go's name-before-type syntax.
Initialise variables in a var declaration and let Go infer each omitted type from its corresponding initialiser.
Use short variable declarations with the colon-equals syntax inside functions, where implicit var declarations are permitted.
Survey Go's boolean, string, integer, floating-point, complex, byte, and rune types, including integer size guidance.
Learn the default zero values assigned to uninitialized Go variables: zero for numbers, false for booleans, and empty text for strings.
Convert values explicitly with type conversion expressions, as Go does not permit implicit assignment between different numeric types.
See how Go infers variable types from typed values and chooses default types for untyped numeric constants according to their precision.
Declare character, string, boolean, and numeric constants with const, noting that short declaration syntax cannot define constants.
Explore high-precision numeric constants and how an untyped constant assumes the type required by its surrounding context.
Mark the end of the current lesson, then return to the module list to select another topic or continue onward.
Learn Go's single looping construct, including the for loop's initialisation, condition, post statement, scope, and required braces.
Simplify a Go for loop by omitting its optional initialisation and post statements while retaining the loop condition.
Express a while-style loop in Go by omitting the initialisation and post statements along with their semicolons.
Create a compact infinite loop in Go by writing a for statement without any loop condition.
Write Go if statements without parentheses around the condition while retaining the language's required braces.
Begin an if statement with a short statement and keep variables declared there scoped through the end of the conditional.
Use values declared by an if short statement throughout its associated if and else branches.
Implement a square-root function with an iterative approximation loop, then refine its stopping condition and compare different initial guesses.
Use Go switch statements as concise conditional chains with automatic case termination and cases that need not be constants or integers.
Understand that switch cases are evaluated from top to bottom and evaluation stops as soon as one case succeeds.
Write a switch without a condition as a clean alternative to a long if-then-else chain, equivalent to switching on true.
Defer a function call until its surrounding function returns while evaluating the deferred call's arguments immediately.
Stack multiple deferred calls and observe their last-in-first-out execution order when the surrounding function returns.
Finish the lesson and either browse the available modules for a new subject or advance to the following lesson.
Work with Go pointers by taking addresses and dereferencing values, while noting nil as the zero value and the absence of pointer arithmetic.
Define a Go struct as a single value composed of a collection of fields.
Access the individual fields of a Go struct using dot notation.
Access fields through a pointer to a struct using convenient dot notation without writing an explicit dereference.
Create struct values with literals, initialise selected fields by name in any order, and use & to obtain a pointer to a struct value.
Declare fixed-length Go arrays whose element count forms part of the array type and cannot be resized.
Create dynamically sized slice views over arrays and select half-open element ranges with low and high bounds.
Understand that slices reference underlying arrays, so element changes are visible through other slices sharing the same storage.
Construct a slice literal using array-literal syntax without specifying a fixed array length.
Omit low or high slice bounds to use zero and the underlying sequence length as their respective defaults.
Distinguish slice length from capacity, inspect both with built-in functions, and reslice only within available capacity.
Recognize nil as a slice's zero value, with no underlying array and both length and capacity equal to zero.
Allocate zeroed arrays and obtain dynamically sized slices with make, optionally specifying a separate capacity.
Build multidimensional data structures by using slices whose elements are themselves slices.
Append elements to a slice and understand when insufficient backing-array space causes allocation of a larger array.
Iterate over slices or maps with range and receive each slice element's index together with a copied value.
Ignore an unwanted range index or value with the blank identifier, or omit the second variable when only the index is needed.
Implement a picture generator that allocates a two-dimensional slice of unsigned bytes and computes values for a displayed image.
Create maps from keys to values with make and understand why a nil map has no keys and cannot accept new entries.
Initialise Go maps with map literals that provide a required key for every value.
Shorten map literals by omitting repeated element types when the top-level element type is a named type.
Insert, update, retrieve, and delete map entries, then use a two-value lookup to distinguish missing keys from zero values.
Implement a word-count function that returns a map recording how many times each word occurs in an input string.
Treat functions as values that can be assigned, passed as function arguments, and returned as results.
Create closures that reference and modify variables outside their bodies, with each returned closure bound to its own state.
Implement a function that returns a closure producing successive numbers in the Fibonacci sequence.
Conclude the completed lesson by choosing a different module from the list or moving forward to the next lesson.
Define methods on Go types using a special receiver argument, providing behaviour without a class system.
See that a Go method is equivalent in behaviour to a regular function whose receiver is written as an ordinary argument.
Declare methods on locally defined non-struct types while respecting the rule that receiver types belong to the same package.
Use pointer receivers when a method must modify its receiver, unlike value receivers that operate on copies.
Rewrite the Abs and Scale methods as ordinary functions, then observe how changing the pointer parameter affects behaviour and what must change for the example to compile.
Call pointer-receiver methods on either values or pointers, with Go interpreting a call on a value such as v.Scale(5) as (&v).Scale(5).
Call value-receiver methods through values or pointers as Go automatically dereferences the pointer for the method invocation.
Choose pointer receivers to permit mutation or avoid copying large values, and use a consistent receiver kind across a type's methods.
Define interfaces as sets of method signatures and see how receiver choice determines whether a value or pointer implements one.
Implement interfaces implicitly by defining their methods, decoupling interface declarations from implementations across packages.
Model an interface value as an underlying concrete value and type, with method calls dispatched to that concrete type.
Distinguish a non-nil interface holding a nil concrete value and design methods that can handle a nil receiver gracefully.
Understand that a nil interface contains neither a value nor a concrete type, making method calls on it a run-time error.
Use the empty interface, or its equivalent any alias, to hold values of arbitrary types in general-purpose code.
Extract an interface's underlying concrete value with a type assertion and use the two-result form to avoid a panic on mismatch.
Use a type switch to test an interface value against several concrete types and bind a correctly typed value in each case.
Implement the Stringer interface so a value can describe itself as text for formatting and printing.
Make an IP address type implement the Stringer interface and format its four components as a dotted-quad address.
Represent failures with Go's built-in error interface, return error values from functions, and test them against nil.
Extend a square-root function to return a custom error for negative inputs and avoid an infinite loop when formatting that error.
Read streams through the Reader interface by filling byte slices and handling the returned byte count, errors, and end-of-stream signal.
Implement a Reader type whose Read method supplies an infinite stream of the ASCII character A.
Wrap another Reader with a custom implementation that transforms alphabetical characters using the ROT13 substitution cipher.
Understand the Image interface through its colour model, bounds, and pixel lookup methods and their associated colour types.
Define a custom image type that implements colour model, rectangular bounds, and pixel colour lookup for generated pictures.
Close out the lesson and decide whether to revisit the module directory or continue directly into the next lesson.
Write generic Go functions with bracketed type parameters and use the comparable constraint for equality-based slice searches.
Define generic types with type parameters, illustrated by a singly linked list capable of storing values of any type.
Acknowledge completion of the lesson before returning to the module catalog or progressing to the lesson that follows.
Start lightweight goroutines, understand where call arguments are evaluated, and synchronise access to shared memory used by concurrent goroutines.
Send and receive typed values through channels, using their default blocking behaviour to synchronise work between goroutines.
Create buffered channels with a fixed capacity and observe sends blocking when full and receives blocking when empty.
Close channels from the sending side, detect closure during receives, and range until all transmitted values are consumed.
Use select to wait for several channel operations, proceeding with a ready case and choosing randomly when multiple cases can run.
Add a default case to select when a channel send or receive should be attempted without blocking.
Frame the problem of comparing differently shaped binary trees that contain the same ordered values using Go channels and concurrency.
Implement a concurrent tree walker and use its channel output to determine whether two binary trees store identical value sequences.
Protect shared state with mutual exclusion by locking and unlocking a mutex, including deferred unlocking for reliable release.
Parallelise a web crawler with Go concurrency while ensuring that no URL is fetched twice and shared map access remains safe.
Continue learning Go through documentation, tutorials, references, talks, codewalks, articles, and resources on concurrency and web applications.
